items.title: 10.7 Lenz's law and direction of induced emf

source_refs.note: Topic 10.7 with Figs. 10.15 and 10.16, Examples 10.6 and 10.7 and the Point to ponder (PDF 240-243, printed 237-240). Example 10.7 is printed on the page before topic 10.8.

blocks.text: In the previous section Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction was written as epsilon = -N delta Phi/delta t. The minus sign in this expression is very important; it relates to the direction of the induced emf. To determine the direction we use a principle based on the discovery made by the Russian physicist Heinrich Lenz in 1834: the polarity of an induced emf always produces an induced current that opposes the change in the magnetic field that caused the emf.

blocks.title: Lenz's law
blocks.text: The direction of the induced current is always such that it opposes the change that caused the current.

Lenz's law specifically applies to induced currents and not directly to induced emf. This means we can apply it to closed conducting loops or coils. If the loop is not closed, we can imagine it closed to determine the direction of the induced current, and from this infer the direction of the induced emf.
Lenz's law with a bar magnet and a coil

Let us apply Lenz's law to a coil in which a current is induced by the movement of a bar magnet. A current-carrying coil generates a magnetic field similar to that of a bar magnet, with one face of the coil acting as a north pole and the other as a south pole. To oppose the motion of the bar magnet, the face of the coil towards the magnet must become a north pole (Fig. 10.15); the two north poles then repel each other. According to the right-hand rule, the induced current in the coil must flow anticlockwise when viewed from the side of the bar magnet. The 'push' of the magnet is the 'change' that produces the induced current, and the current acts to oppose the push. On the other hand, if we pull the magnet away from the coil, the induced current opposes the 'pull' by creating a south pole on the face of the coil towards the bar magnet.

Right: the coil with its own field lines; the axial line runs from B on the right to N on the left, so the face towards the magnet is N. The coil's ends join a galvanometer circuit with current arrows, labelled current is anticlockwise.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.15: A bar magnet pushed towards a coil: the face of the coil towards the magnet becomes a north pole (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.15).

blocks.text: Lenz's law and the conservation of energy

Lenz's law is also a manifestation of the law of conservation of energy and can be conveniently applied to circuits involving induced currents. Revisit the experiment of Fig. 10.16. When the rod moves to the right, an emf is induced in it, causing an induced current to flow through the loop anticlockwise. Because the current-carrying rod is moving within the magnetic field, it experiences a magnetic force Fm of magnitude ILB sin 90 degrees. By the right-hand rule the direction of Fm is opposite to the velocity v, so it tends to stop the rod (Fig. 10.16a). To keep the rod moving with constant velocity, an external force equal in magnitude to Fm but opposite in direction must be applied; this external force provides the energy needed for the induced current to flow. Thus electromagnetic induction obeys the law of conservation of energy.

blocks.alt: Two panels of a rod on rails closed by a galvanometer, B into paper. (a) Current I runs up the rod, left along the top rail and right along the bottom rail (anticlockwise); the magnetic force F_m points left, opposite to the velocity v, and a hand pulls the rod. (b) Current I runs down the rod and the rail arrows are reversed (clockwise); F_m points right, along v.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.16: (a) Induced current anticlockwise: F_m opposes v; (b) the clockwise case forbidden by Lenz's law (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.16).

blocks.text: Lenz's law forbids the induced current from flowing clockwise in this case, because the force Fm would then be in the direction of v and would accelerate the rod to the right (Fig. 10.16b). This in turn would induce a stronger current, the magnetic force due to it would also increase, and the motion of the rod would be accelerated more and more. Starting with a minute quantity of energy we would obtain an ever-increasing kinetic energy of motion, apparently from nowhere; the process would become self-perpetuating, which is against the law of conservation of energy.

blocks.title: Example 10.6
blocks.text: A metal rod of length 25 cm moves at a speed of 0.5 m s^-1 perpendicular to a 0.25 T magnetic field. Find the emf produced in the rod. Solution: v = 0.5 m s^-1, L = 25 cm = 0.25 m, B = 0.25 T = 0.25 N A^-1 m^-1. epsilon = vBL = 0.5 m s^-1 x 0.25 N A^-1 m^-1 x 0.25 m = 3.13 x 10^-2 J C^-1 = 3.13 x 10^-2 V.

blocks.title: Example 10.7
blocks.text: A loop of wire is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.6 T perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The area of the loop begins to shrink at a constant rate delta A/delta t = 0.8 m^2 s^-1. What is the magnitude of the emf induced in the loop while it is shrinking? Solution: N = 1, B = 0.6 T. Rate of change of flux = delta phi/delta t = B (delta A/delta t) cos 0 = B delta A/delta t. By Faraday's law the magnitude of the emf is epsilon = N delta phi/delta t = N B delta A/delta t = 1 x 0.6 N A^-1 m^-1 x 0.8 m^2 s^-1 = 0.48 J C^-1 = 0.48 V.
